steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction
1. Fires
- magnitude + frequency of wildland fires increasing in Western US
- "megafires": threat to environment, human life, property, resources
- "type conversions": dominant vegetation (forestry) replaced by new vegetation (grasses); hotter, less moisture -> more fire-prone
- social: smoke harms respiratory health; economic burden of structural damage
- study factors of severity and spread -> communities allocate time/resources, minimize losses

2. Burn severity
- metric: post-fire damage to soil and vegetation
- influenced by fuel availability/flammability, environmental stressors, topography
- plant water stress variables important; pre-season soil moisture strong predictor
- ECOSTRESS satellite: high spatial + temporal resolution hydrological info: evapotranspiration (ET), evaporative stress index (ESI), water use efficiency (WUE)
- hypothesis: they increase predictability of burn severity
- higher ET where more plant productivity / fuel; ESI = moisture available to vegetation -> flammability; WUE -> vulnerability to climatic stressors
- complex relationships -> spatial patterns; research attention in recent decades

3. Models
- physics-based simulations: time dependent, numerical CFD; Jain: unfeasible at large scales, often low accuracy
- empirical/statistical models: need nonlinear relationships -> complexity
- ML: independent of physical processes, learns from data
- "base learners" used: RF, Maximum Entropy, ANNs, Decision Trees, SVM, Genetic Algorithms

4. Ensembles
- Basic Complex fire (2008), Big-Sur: RF vs GPR vs SVM vs multiple regression; RF best, 48% less error than Linear Regression; likely ensemble learning
- ensemble learning = merge base learners for one problem; ensembles beat individual learners; better when base learners accurate + diverse
- burn severity with ensembles relatively unexplored
- our model: Super Learner (SL) ensemble + spatial autocorrelation; not yet done for burn severity

5. ML + spatial statistics
- ML alone: limited on geostatistics errors like data gaps; many cannot estimate prediction/classification error
- ways: account for spatial correlation after ML; or inside ML (RF)
- Li: RF + Ordinary Kriging best of 23 methods
- Multi-layer Neural Network with spatial relationships beat ordinal Kriging and plain network at new locations; Neural Networks + Kriging also helpful
- mixed spatial ML model: RF + Gaussian processes for spatial autocorrelation; better than RF alone
- Davies: SL with Kriging in base learner library; SL as good or better than best base learner
- Kriging + SL optimized separately -> accurate geological attributes
- our data strongly spatially correlated -> expect spatial correction to help SL

6. Study
- four wildfires, 2019-2021
- Kincade, San Mateo–Santa Cruz Unit (CZU) Lightning Complex: Northern Pacific Coast; warm/hot summer Mediterranean climate
- Windy, Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Park (KNP) Complex: Sierra Nevada, inland mid-latitudes; dry summer subarctic climate
- questions: relate intense burn to vegetation, weather, topography? SL accurate across California? most important variables?
- outline: data Section 2, methods Section 3, results Section 4, conclusion Section 5

## Introduction

Current trends show that wildland fires in the Western US are increasing in magnitude and frequency. In recent years “megafires” have risen, and they are a threat to the environment, human life, property, and resources. Wildland fires disturb microclimates because they cause “type conversions” of landscapes, where the vegetation that once dominated (such as forestry) gets replaced with new vegetation (such as grasses). These “type conversions” make the conditions for wildland fires worse, because the landscape becomes hotter and has less moisture. This is an ecological threat but it also has dangerous social implications. For one, wildland fire smoke is proven to be bad for respiratory health. Also, communities have to bear the economic burden of recovering from devastating structural damages. So studying the factors that influence how severe burn incidents are and how they spread has reached a critical point. If we understand what drives wildland fires, communities can allocate their time and resources effectively to minimize losses.

Burn severity is a metric used to evaluate the damage to soil and vegetation after a fire. It is influenced by how available and flammable the fuels are, by environmental stressors, and by topography. Previous studies show that plant water stress variables are important for predicting burn severity. There is also evidence that pre-season soil moisture is a strong predictor. The ECOsystem and Spaceborne Thermal Radiometer Experiment on Space Station (ECOSTRESS) satellite gives data with high spatial and temporal resolution on hydrological information like evapotranspiration (ET), evaporative stress index (ESI), and water use efficiency (WUE). We include these variables in our study since they are relevant for characterizing fuel amount and flammability, and we hypothesize that they will increase how predictable burn severity is. Regions that have greater plant productivity, and so more fire fuel, tend to have higher ET. ESI evaluates the moisture available to vegetation, so it is an indicator of how flammable those fuels are. And WUE measurements give insight into how vulnerable plants are to climatic stressors. The relationship between these factors is complex and it influences the spatial patterns of burn severity. Because of this complexity, predicting the spatial patterns of burn severity has got the attention of researchers in recent decades.

Traditional physics-based simulations that capture the physical processes have challenges. These simulators are time dependent and they rely on numerical solutions to computational fluid dynamics. Jain reports that such models are unfeasible to apply on large scales and often have low accuracy. To get around these issues, many wildland fire researchers use empirical and statistical models instead. But this means modelling nonlinear relationships, which brings complexity. Machine learning (ML) has come up as a contemporary approach in wildland fire research. It does not depend on implementing the physical processes, instead it learns from the data directly. Many ML methods, which we call “base learners” from here on, have been applied to predicting wildland fires, including Random Forests (RF), Maximum Entropy, Artificial Neural Networks, Decision Trees, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Genetic Algorithms.

- ensemble learning = merge base learners; beats individual learners; better when accurate + diverse; little used for burn severity
- our model: Super Learner (SL) + spatial autocorrelation (not yet done for burn severity)
- ML alone: limited on geostatistical errors like data gaps; often no prediction/classification error estimates
- spatial correlation after ML, or inside ML (RF); Li: RF + Ordinary Kriging best of 23 methods; Multi-layer Neural Network with spatial relationships beat ordinal Kriging + plain network; Neural Networks + Kriging also helpful
- mixed spatial ML: RF + Gaussian processes, better than RF alone; Davies: SL with Kriging in library, as good or better than best base learner; Kriging + SL separately -> accurate geological attributes
- expect spatial correction to help our SL
- four fires 2019-2021: Kincade, CZU Lightning Complex (Northern Pacific Coast, warm/hot summer Mediterranean); Windy, KNP Complex (Sierra Nevada, dry summer subarctic)
- questions: intense burn vs vegetation/weather/topography; SL accuracy across California; most important variables
- outline: Sections 2-5

## Introduction

Current trends show that wildland fires in the Western US are increasing in magnitude and frequency. In recent years “megafires” have risen, and they are a threat to the environment, human life, property, and resources. Wildland fires disturb microclimates because they cause “type conversions” of landscapes, where the vegetation that once dominated (such as forestry) gets replaced with new vegetation (such as grasses). These “type conversions” make the conditions for wildland fires worse, because the landscape becomes hotter and has less moisture. This is an ecological threat but it also has dangerous social implications. For one, wildland fire smoke is proven to be bad for respiratory health. Also, communities have to bear the economic burden of recovering from devastating structural damages. So studying the factors that influence how severe burn incidents are and how they spread has reached a critical point. If we understand what drives wildland fires, communities can allocate their time and resources effectively to minimize losses.

Burn severity is a metric used to evaluate the damage to soil and vegetation after a fire. It is influenced by how available and flammable the fuels are, by environmental stressors, and by topography. Previous studies show that plant water stress variables are important for predicting burn severity. There is also evidence that pre-season soil moisture is a strong predictor. The ECOsystem and Spaceborne Thermal Radiometer Experiment on Space Station (ECOSTRESS) satellite gives data with high spatial and temporal resolution on hydrological information like evapotranspiration (ET), evaporative stress index (ESI), and water use efficiency (WUE). We include these variables in our study since they are relevant for characterizing fuel amount and flammability, and we hypothesize that they will increase how predictable burn severity is. Regions that have greater plant productivity, and so more fire fuel, tend to have higher ET. ESI evaluates the moisture available to vegetation, so it is an indicator of how flammable those fuels are. And WUE measurements give insight into how vulnerable plants are to climatic stressors. The relationship between these factors is complex and it influences the spatial patterns of burn severity. Because of this complexity, predicting the spatial patterns of burn severity has got the attention of researchers in recent decades.

Traditional physics-based simulations that capture the physical processes have challenges. These simulators are time dependent and they rely on numerical solutions to computational fluid dynamics. Jain reports that such models are unfeasible to apply on large scales and often have low accuracy. To get around these issues, many wildland fire researchers use empirical and statistical models instead. But this means modelling nonlinear relationships, which brings complexity. Machine learning (ML) has come up as a contemporary approach in wildland fire research. It does not depend on implementing the physical processes, instead it learns from the data directly. Many ML methods, which we call “base learners” from here on, have been applied to predicting wildland fires, including Random Forests (RF), Maximum Entropy, Artificial Neural Networks, Decision Trees, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Genetic Algorithms.

One study of the Basic Complex fire (2008) in Big-Sur, California compared RF, Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), and SVM with multiple regression for assessing burn severity. RF did the best and reduced model error by 48% compared to Linear Regression, and this is probably because of its ensemble learning approach. Ensemble learning merges multiple base learners to solve one learning problem. Using ensemble ML models to predict burn severity is still relatively unexplored so far. The current literature says ensemble learning outperforms individual learners, and when the base algorithms are accurate and diverse the performance is even better. Our model will use a Super Learner (SL) ensemble algorithm, which aggregates diverse base learners, to forecast wildland burn severity. Our model will also account for spatial autocorrelation. As far as we know this has not been done yet for predicting burn severity.

We are motivated to combine ensemble prediction and spatial modeling by the current literature, which shows that combining ML algorithms with traditional spatial statistics methods is effective. With spatially-dependent data, ML algorithms on their own are limited in accounting for common errors in geostatistics like data gaps. Also, unlike geostatistical methods, many common machine learning algorithms cannot give estimates of the prediction or classification error.

Using a ML algorithm together with a statistical method is likely more applicable to spatially-correlated data and gives stronger predictions. The current literature shows spatial prediction used together with diverse ML algorithms. A spatial ML model can be implemented in multiple ways: one is to account for spatial correlation after running the ML algorithm. Another is to try to account for spatial correlation inside the ML algorithm, such as Random Forest. Li found that combining Random Forest and Ordinary Kriging (a form of spatial prediction) gave the best results out of 23 methods. Another study got the most accurate predictions at new locations by training a Multi-layer Neural Network that includes spatial relationships, compared to just ordinal Kriging and a normal Multi-layer Neural Network. A third study also found benefits from combining Neural Networks and Kriging for spatial prediction.

One study proposed a mixed spatial ML model that uses a RF machine learning algorithm and accounts for spatial autocorrelation with a Gaussian processes. This mixed-model approach was better than RF alone on spatially correlated data. Davies looks at using an ensemble ML algorithm that has Kriging in its base learner library. Their results also confirmed the mixed-method approach is favorable, finding that SL performs as good or better than the best base learner in spatial prediction. Another study found that optimizing the predictions from Kriging and SL separately gave accurate estimation of geological attributes. Since our wildland fire datasets have strong geospatial correlation, we expect that accounting for spatial correlation on the ensemble predictions will make our SL model more predictive.

In this study we look at the spatial pattern of burn severity of four wildfires between 2019-2021. Two of them, the Kincade and the San Mateo–Santa Cruz Unit (CZU) Lightning Complex fire, represent fires along the Northern Pacific Coast in California. This territory has a warm/hot summer Mediterranean climate. The other two, the Windy and the Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Park (KNP) Complex, represent fires in the Sierra Nevada region, which covers most of the inland mid-latitudes of California. This region has a dry summer subarctic climate. The questions that motivate this paper are:

- How can we relate areas of intense burn to vegetation, weather, and topography?

- Can a Super Learner algorithm accurately predict post-wildfire burn severity throughout California?

- Which variables are most important to burn severity?

The rest of the paper goes as follows. Section 2 describes the wildland fire data. Section 3 introduces the methods and computational algorithms. Section 4 summarizes the results, and Section 5 concludes.

## Introduction

Current trends reveal an increase in the magnitude and frequency of wildland fires in the Western US [1]. The rise of “megafires” in recent years poses a threat to the environment, human life, property, and resources [2]. Wildland fires disturb microclimates by causing “type conversions” of landscapes [3], where once dominant vegetation (such as forestry) is replaced with new vegetation (such as grasses). “Type conversions” intensify the conditions conducive to wildland fires by creating a hotter landscape with less moisture [3]. Not only is this an ecological threat, it also has dangerous social implications. For one, wildland fire smoke has proven detrimental to respiratory health [4]. Furthermore, communities bear the economic burden of recovering from devastating structural damages. Therefore, studying the factors that influence the severity and spread of burn incidents has reached a critical point. By understanding the drivers of wildland fires, communities can effectively allocate their time and resources to minimize losses.

Burn severity is a metric used to evaluate post-fire damage to soil and vegetation [5]. It is influenced by the availability and flammability of fuels, environmental stressors, and topography [2]. Previous studies have shown that plant water stress variables are important for predicting burn severity [6], and there is also evidence that pre-season soil moisture is a strong predictor [7]. Data from the ECOsystem and Spaceborne Thermal Radiometer Experiment on Space Station (ECOSTRESS) satellite [8] provides high spatial and temporal resolution of hydrological information such as evapotranspiration (ET), evaporative stress index (ESI), and water use efficiency (WUE). We incorporate these variables into our study because of their relevance in characterizing fuel amount and flammability, and we hypothesize that they will increase the predictability of burn severity. Regions with greater plant productivity, and more fire fuel, tend to have higher measures of ET [9]. Moreover, ESI, which evaluates the moisture available to vegetation, serves as an indicator of the flammability of those fuels [10]. Finally, WUE measurements provide insight into the vulnerability of plants to climatic stressors [6]. The complex relationship between these factors influences the spatial patterns of burn severity [11]. Because of this complexity, predicting the spatial patterns of burn severity has drawn the attention of researchers in recent decades.

Traditional physics-based simulations that capture physical processes [12] pose challenges. These simulators are time dependent and rely on numerical solutions to computational fluid dynamics. Jain [13] reports that such models are unfeasible to apply on large scales and often produce low accuracy. To overcome these issues, many wildland fire researchers turn to empirical and statistical models, which, however, require modelling nonlinear relationships and so introduce complexity. Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a contemporary approach in wildland fire research. It is independent of the implementation of physical processes and instead learns directly from data [13]. Many ML methods, henceforth referred to as “base learners,” have been applied to wildland fire prediction, including Random Forests (RF), Maximum Entropy, Artificial Neural Networks, Decision Trees, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Genetic Algorithms [13].

A study of the Basic Complex fire (2008) in Big-Sur, California compared the performance of RF, Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), and SVM to multiple regression in assessing burn severity. RF performed best and reduced model error by 48% compared to Linear Regression, likely due to its ensemble learning approach [14]. Ensemble learning merges multiple base learners to solve a single learning problem [15]. To date, the use of ensemble ML models to predict burn severity remains relatively unexplored. Current literature indicates that ensemble learning outperforms individual learners [16], and performance is further enhanced when base algorithms are accurate and diverse [15]. Our model will incorporate a Super Learner (SL) ensemble algorithm [17], which aggregates diverse base learners, to forecast wildland burn severity. In addition, our model will account for spatial autocorrelation, which to the best of our knowledge has yet to be done for predicting burn severity.

Our motivation for combining ensemble prediction and spatial modeling comes from current literature showing the effectiveness of combining ML algorithms with traditional spatial statistics methods. When handling spatially-dependent data, ML algorithms alone are limited in their ability to account for common errors in geostatistics such as data gaps [18]. Furthermore, unlike geostatistical methods, many common machine learning algorithms cannot provide estimates of prediction or classification error [18].

Applying a ML algorithm together with a statistical method is likely to be more applicable to spatially-correlated data and to yield stronger predictions, and current literature shows spatial prediction used in tandem with diverse ML algorithms. There are multiple ways to implement a spatial ML model; one is to account for spatial correlation after implementing the ML algorithm [19]. Another is to account for spatial correlation within the ML algorithm, such as Random Forest [20]. Li [21] found that a combination of Random Forest and Ordinary Kriging (a form of spatial prediction) gave the best results out of 23 methods. [22] obtained the most accurate predictions at new locations after training a Multi-layer Neural Network that includes spatial relationships, compared to ordinal Kriging alone and a normal Multi-layer Neural Network. [23] also found benefits from combining Neural Networks and Kriging for spatial prediction.

A mixed spatial ML model was proposed by [24] that incorporates a RF machine learning algorithm and accounts for spatial autocorrelation using a Gaussian processes; this mixed-model approach proved superior to RF alone on spatially correlated data. Davies [25] examines an ensemble ML algorithm that includes Kriging in its base learner library. Their results further confirmed the favorability of a mixed-method approach, finding that SL performs as good as or better than the best base learner in spatial prediction. Another study found that optimizing the predictions from Kriging and SL separately provided accurate estimation of geological attributes [26]. Because there is strong geospatial correlation in our wildland fire datasets, we expect that accounting for spatial correlation on the ensemble predictions will enhance the predictability of our SL model.

In this study, we investigate the spatial pattern of burn severity of four wildfires between 2019-2021. Two fires, the Kincade and San Mateo–Santa Cruz Unit (CZU) Lightning Complex fire, represent fires along the Northern Pacific Coast in California [27], a territory characterized by a warm/hot summer Mediterranean climate. In contrast, the Windy and Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Park (KNP) Complex represent fires in the Sierra Nevada region, which spans most of the inland mid-latitudes of California [28] and has a dry summer subarctic climate. This paper is motivated by the questions:

- How can we relate areas of intense burn to vegetation, weather, and topography?

- Can a Super Learner algorithm accurately predict post-wildfire burn severity throughout California?

- Which variables are most important to burn severity?

The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. The wildland fire data are described in Section 2. Section 3 introduces the methods and computational algorithms. The results are summarized in Section 4, and Section 5 concludes.
